The bristles splay and spring back with real hair behaviour; the pigment is genuinely wet, sitting proud, pooling at edges and thinning at the end of a stroke. The ceramic fragments have true weight and grate audibly when pushed. Hard raking light from one side, skimming across the glaze to reveal the craquelure and the ridges of the paint, with deep black falloff everywhere else. PIECE 6 IN DETAIL — the piece with no writing:
It carries no letters and no flowers. Instead, across its whole surface, a bold TRIBAL TATTOO DESIGN painted in solid cobalt blue: thick interlocking black-work shapes, long pointed spikes and curved barbs, sharp hooks and tapering flame-like tips, the symmetrical geometry of a nineties tribal armband tattoo, filling the fragment edge to edge and running right off its broken edges as if the design continued onto the pieces that are missing. The strokes are broad, filled solid and hard-edged, with no shading and no fine detail — much heavier, blacker and more graphic than the delicate china patterns on the other five pieces. It looks like a tattoo that has been put onto a dinner plate, and it is the strangest thing in the picture.

HOW EACH PIECE IS DIFFERENT AS AN OBJECT:
Each of the six is a different white — one bone white, one warm ivory, one cold blue-white, one greyish, one very bright, one yellowed with age. Each has a different blue pattern around its edge — one has a fine lace border, one has a row of squares, one has painted flowers, one has a plain blue line, one has nothing, one is worn away. Some are glossy, some are dull, one is covered in a fine web of old cracks stained brown.
THEY DO NOT FIT PROPERLY. The pieces are different thicknesses, so some sit slightly higher than their neighbours and cast small hard shadows onto them. The edges do not line up. There are narrow black gaps between all of them. The outer circle is subtly wrong, not a perfect circle. Nothing is glued and nothing is repaired.
The broken edges are raw, dry and chalky white, with tiny crumbs of ceramic dust along them. No gold anywhere.

A vertical 2:3 film poster. Photographed straight down from directly above. Dead centre on a dark surface, one round plate, made of SIX BROKEN PIECES FROM SIX DIFFERENT PLATES joined together into a circle WITH GOLD. Deep darkness all around it.

THINK OF IT AS A RANSOM NOTE MADE OF PORCELAIN, REPAIRED IN GOLD: every piece comes from a different plate, painted by a different person, in a different style of lettering — and someone has bonded them all together with molten gold to make one object.

Read across the pieces, the plate says, in cobalt blue, on two lines:
"AZUL"
"COBALTO"
These are the only words in the picture. Spelling exactly: A-Z-U-L and C-O-B-A-L-T-O. No letter appears twice.

THE SIX PIECES, one by one:

PIECE 1 — upper left. A curved arc piece filling the top-left quarter of the circle, from the nine o'clock position round to twelve o'clock.
Its plate: thin, bone white, glossy new glaze, clean and unworn. Around its outer rim runs a fine delicate blue lace border, like knitted thread.
Its letters: "AZ" — the first half of the top word. Spiky pointed gothic letters, sharp and narrow, with thin curling tails coming off them. Painted confidently with a fine brush in dark saturated blue.

PIECE 2 — upper right. The mirror arc, from twelve o'clock round to three o'clock, completing the top of the circle.
Its plate: old and yellowed warm ivory, its whole surface covered in a fine web of tiny cracks stained brown with age. Its rim is moulded with a row of small raised beads. Around the rim, a band of small blue squares in a repeating row.
Its letters: "UL" — the second half of the top word. Fat heavy blocky letters, blunt and square-cornered, the same thickness all the way round, no decoration at all, like a rubber stamp pressed into the glaze. A greyer, duller blue than the others.
This piece is noticeably thicker than the rest and sits about two millimetres higher than piece 1 beside it, so the gold seam between them is built up thick and steep to bridge the step.

PIECE 3 — middle left. A piece filling the left flank of the circle, below piece 1.
Its plate: cold blue-white, very bright and very glossy, with no border pattern at all — completely bare around the rim. Its outer edge is chipped in two places, and both chips have been filled in with gold.
Its letters: "CO" — the start of the bottom word. Thin spidery slanted handwriting, fine as a pen line, with long looping tails trailing from each letter. Pale watery blue, so faint it almost disappears where the light falls off.

PIECE 4 — middle centre. The big piece in the heart of the plate, between pieces 3 and 5. This is the largest fragment of the six.
Its plate: greyish white with a dull matte surface, no shine at all. It is an inner fragment so it has no rim and no border pattern — just a bare field with one rubbed patch where something has been scrubbed off.
Its letters: "BAL" — the middle of the bottom word. Plain simple clean capitals, perfectly even thickness, absolutely no decoration, machine-regular. Very dark saturated blue. These letters are much bigger and much heavier than every other letter on the plate — crude, blunt and obvious next to the delicate ones around them.

PIECE 5 — middle right. A piece filling the right flank of the circle, below piece 2.
Its plate: very white, high gloss, its outer rim scalloped in soft waves. Around the rim, painted blue peony flowers with leaves, one area rubbed almost blank with use.
Its letters: "TO" — the end of the bottom word. Very ornate letters, thick strokes right beside hairline strokes, covered in small painted curls and swashes trailing off every corner. Medium blue, painted slowly and carefully.

PIECE 6 — bottom. A wide arc filling the whole lower third of the circle.
Its plate: heavy thick ceramic in a greenish-grey white, deeply stained brown in the crazing from years of use. A plain wide rim with one thick blue line around it.
Its letters: NONE. This piece carries no writing at all — only one large painted blue flower spray across it. It is the quiet piece.

THE GOLD — the repair is the second subject of the picture:
Every join between the six pieces is filled and sealed with gold. The seams are rivers of real metallic gold lacquer running through the plate: bright, warm, mirror-polished, slightly raised above the surface of the porcelain, with rounded glossy edges where the molten gold pooled and set. Their width is uneven — thin as a hair in places, swelling to several millimetres where the fragments did not fit, and building up thick and lumpy at the steps where one piece sits higher than its neighbour. The gold laps a little way over the glaze on either side of each join, and a few small gold droplets have run and hardened where it overflowed. The two chips in piece 3 are filled with solid gold, and a few tiny hairline cracks branch off the main seams in fine gold threads.
Where a seam crosses a letter, the gold cuts straight through the blue stroke and the letter continues on the far side — the words read across the gold veins, unbroken and completely legible.
There are no black gaps anywhere: every space between the pieces is gold. Nothing is left open, nothing is glued with anything else, nothing is hidden. The repair is proud of itself.

HOW THEY FIT TOGETHER:
Badly, and the gold is what makes it work. The six are different thicknesses, so some sit higher than their neighbours. The rim curves do not continue into each other, so the outer circle is subtly wrong and lumpy, not a perfect circle. Six strangers held together by gold and photographed.
The two lines of writing still line up across all the joins, so the words read straight and clean even though the pieces do not fit.

THE LIGHT:
One single hard light from the upper left, low and raking across the plate. No fill light, no softbox. Every piece throws a hard black-edged shadow. The light dies fast — the corners of the frame are almost completely black. Strong vignette. The whole image is underexposed by one stop: nothing is bright white, the shadows have no detail in them.
The raking light hits the raised gold seams edge-on and they blaze: a network of hot bright metallic highlights running across a dark cold plate, the brightest thing in the entire frame by a wide margin. On the shadowed side of each seam the gold goes deep brown-bronze and almost black.

THE COLOUR:
Almost no colour: cobalt blue and six barely different whites, with blacks crushed very slightly green-cyan. The GOLD is the only warm thing in the image — and it is the only warm thing anywhere, which is why it dominates. No orange light, no amber lamps, no warm ambience: the warmth comes from the metal itself.

Macro sharp everywhere, no blur, no bokeh. Dust on the glaze, a smeared fingerprint catching the light, hairline scratches, ceramic grit, tiny polishing marks in the gold. It looks like a real repaired antique photographed as evidence on an examination table. Fine film grain.

Across the three fragments, painted in deep cobalt blue, exactly two words on exactly two lines, centred, one word per line:
"AZUL"
"COBALTO"
Nothing else is written anywhere. The spelling is exactly A-Z-U-L and C-O-B-A-L-T-O.

THE THREE PIECES — cut the circle into three clear parts with two roughly vertical fracture lines, so the plate reads as LEFT piece, CENTRE piece, RIGHT piece, each running the full height of the circle. Each piece carries part of both lines of text:
— LEFT piece carries "AZ" on the top line and "COB" on the bottom line.
— CENTRE piece carries "U" on the top line and "AL" on the bottom line.
— RIGHT piece carries "L" on the top line and "TO" on the bottom line.
Read across all three, the two lines say AZUL and COBALTO, complete and perfectly legible. The letters are sized and positioned so the words line up across the joins without any gap in the reading, even though each piece was painted by a different hand on a different plate.

THREE DIFFERENT TYPEFACES — one per fragment, and the clash between them is the whole point:
— On the LEFT piece: an ornate high-contrast serif with blackletter influence — sharp pointed spurs, pinched counters, thick stems against hairline strokes, fine calligraphic flourishes and small curls of scrollwork trailing off the terminals. Painted with a fine brush, cobalt pooling at the stroke ends.
— On the CENTRE piece: a heavy Victorian slab serif — wide, blunt, mechanical, thick square bracketed serifs, almost no stroke contrast, the letterforms flat and evenly weighted like a transfer print rather than a brushstroke, in a slightly greyer, colder blue.
— On the RIGHT piece: a fine copperplate script capital form — steeply angled, extremely thin hairlines against swelling downstrokes, long elegant swashes curling from the letters, drawn with a pointed pen rather than a brush, in a paler, more transparent wash of cobalt.
All three are unmistakably different hands, different eras and different tools, sitting inside one word.

THREE DIFFERENT PLATES — the fragments do not match, and the mismatch is visible everywhere:
— the LEFT fragment is bone white with a glossy modern glaze and a plain narrow rim, its border a delicate cobalt filigree;
— the CENTRE fragment is older and warmer ivory, its glaze finely crazed with a web of crackle stained brown-grey by age, its rim moulded with gadrooning, its border a geometric key-fret band;
— the RIGHT fragment is cooler and bluer white, thicker and heavier ceramic, its rim scalloped, its border a loose floral peony spray, one small area worn where the pattern has rubbed away.
Their thicknesses do not agree: at the joins one edge sits fractionally higher than its neighbour, casting a fine hard shadow onto the piece beside it. The curves of their rims do not quite continue into each other, so the outer circle is subtly wrong. Narrow black gaps of a few millimetres run along both fracture lines. The broken edges are raw, dry and matte — unglazed ceramic, chalky, each fragment a slightly different shade of white in the break, with a fine scatter of porcelain crumbs and pale dust caught along them. No gold, no adhesive, nothing repaired: three strangers pressed together and photographed.

THE LETTERING OVERFLOWS THE PLATE — this is the key idea:
The two words are painted much larger than the plate itself, so the plate is not their support but an accident lying in the middle of them. The words are centred on the plate and their middles fall across its glazed face, but both lines run WIDER than the plate's diameter: the outer letters and all the calligraphic flourishes continue straight past the rim and are painted directly onto the dark table surface around it, in the same cobalt blue, in one continuous unbroken act of writing. The brush clearly did not stop at the edge of the plate. Both words remain complete and completely legible across plate and table.
The paint behaves differently on the two surfaces, and this difference is visible and precise: on the glaze it is glossy, translucent and pooled, floating on a slick white ground; on the dark matte table it is drier, flatter and more absorbed, gripping the texture of the surface, a shade deeper. Where each stroke crosses the raised rim of the plate the paint thins and skips over the ridge, then thickens again on the far side — a tiny visible stutter at every crossing.

THE BREAK: the plate has been broken into six or seven large clean pieces and laid back down in its own shape, the fragments separated by narrow black gaps of a few millimetres, like an exploded diagram of itself. The circle is still unmistakably a circle. The break lines run right through the lettering — one crosses "AZUL" between the Z and the U, another cuts diagonally through "COBALTO" — so the painted strokes are interrupted by black slots wherever they pass a gap, and the words are still completely readable. Two small chips have come away entirely and rest outside the circle, each carrying a fragment of a letter on it, sitting a few centimetres from where it belongs. The broken edges are raw, dry and matte — unglazed ceramic fracture, chalky and slightly warmer white than the glazed face, with a fine scatter of porcelain crumbs and pale dust caught along them. No gold, no adhesive, nothing repaired.

THE LETTERFORMS: hand-painted in classical Spanish ceramic tradition — an ornate serif with blackletter influence, high contrast between thick strokes and hairlines, sharp pointed spurs, small pinched counters, faintly gothic but still readable as a Roman serif. Fine calligraphic flourishes curl off the terminals of the A, the L and the O — and it is these flourishes, the longest and thinnest strokes, that reach furthest out onto the dark table, thin cobalt hairlines and small curls of scrollwork trailing away from the plate into the darkness and fading as the light falls off. Tiny pooling of cobalt at the stroke ends, faint pigment bleed under the glaze on the plate, dry brush texture on the table. "COBALTO" is set slightly wider than "AZUL" so both lines optically fill the same width. A delicate cobalt filigree border follows the rim of the plate, interrupted by the breaks, sitting underneath and behind the big letters that cross over it.
